Rashi on Zevachim 14a:6:1.hebrew: שאי אפשר לבטלה: דלאו אורח ארעא לשחוט בהיכל, ועל כרחו הוא שוחטו בעזרה ומוליכה בהיכל לקרנות מזבח פנימי ולהזאת פרוכת.
Rashi on Zevachim 14a:6:1.english: That it is indispensable: Because it is not respectful to slaughter an animal in the Sanctuary, and perforce, one must slaughter it in the Temple courtyard and convey it into the Sanctuary for the corners of the inner altar and for sprinkling on the curtain.

Steinsaltz comment #1 on Zevachim 14a:19.english: If a person disqualified from the priesthood conveyed the blood, whether at the beginning (where a priest conveyed it afterward) or at the end (where a priest conveyed it at the beginning), the offering is disqualified. This is in accordance with the conclusion of the sugya (Rambam, Sefer Avoda, Hilkhot Pesulei HaMukdashin 1:27).

Steinsaltz comment #2 on Zevachim 14a:19.english: The Amora (in this restricted sense) is identical to the Meturgeman in Mishnaic language. The Meturgeman in the Sages’ lectures was usually a Sage (and sometimes even an important Sage) whose role was to translate the Sage’s words from Hebrew to Aramaic, and also to say them loudly (so sometimes there was more than one Meturgeman, if they needed to make it heard to many). Often, the Meturgeman would not only translate but also explain, for the Sage would state the main ideas, while the Meturgeman would elaborate and develop them. And for this reason, the Sages of the Talmud called themselves Amoraim, as they saw their role as a kind of interpreters in this sense for the Sages of the Mishna.

Steinsaltz on Zevachim 14a:19.english: Abaye said to Rav Ḥisda’s interpreter: He asked Rav Ḥisda: What is the halakha with regard to a non-priest (one who is not a priest) conveying the blood? Is it disqualified, like other rites?

Zevachim 14a:19.english: Abaye said to Rav Ḥisda’s interpreter: Ask Rav Ḥisda: What is the halakha with regard to a non-priest conveying the blood? Is the offering disqualified, like other sacrificial rites?

Zevachim 14a:6.english: Rabbi Shimon deems the offering fit if the prohibited intent was during the rite of conveying the blood to the altar. Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish says: Rabbi Shimon concedes that prohibited intent during the conveying of the blood of inner sin offerings disqualifies them, since with regard to those offerings, it is an indispensable rite. Because the blood must be sprinkled inside the Sanctuary and an inner sin offering cannot be slaughtered inside the Sanctuary, conveying the blood into the Sanctuary is always necessary for such offerings.
